entities.summary:
Philon, an eminent Athenian architect of the late 4th century BCE, stands as a pivotal figure in the transition of Classical Greek monumental construction, particularly under the dynamic political leadership of Lycurgus. His contributions, primarily the grand portico of the Telesterion at Eleusis and the formidable Arsenal of Piraeus, exemplify the sophisticated engineering and aesthetic principles of the era, showcasing Athens' enduring commitment to public works and naval supremacy. His work provides invaluable insight into the administrative and architectural practices that defined the city's golden age.

Philon's architectural prowess is most notably documented through two monumental projects. At Eleusis, he designed the twelve-columned Doric portico for the great Hall of the Mysteries (Telesterion), a sacred structure central to the Eleusinian Mysteries, one of the most significant religious rites of the ancient world. This addition enhanced the ceremonial grandeur and structural integrity of the complex. More extensively known, thanks to a detailed inscription (IG II² 1668), is the Arsenal (Skeuotheke) he constructed in Piraeus between 330 and 323 BCE, under the stewardship of Lycurgus. This vast naval storehouse, designed to hold the rigging and equipment for 100 galleys, measured approximately 130 meters long and 18 meters wide, featuring a complex wooden roof system.
